Practical field guide · 45 algorithm families

Machine learning algorithms, and when to use them

A catalogue of learning approaches, problem types and algorithm families. Each one gets a plain-language definition, the formula, an input-to-output flow, runnable Python, and a picture of what it actually does. Every chart here was made by fitting that method to real data when the page was built, and methods in the same section share one dataset, so the only thing that changes between two panels is the algorithm itself.

The distinction that organises everything. A learning approach describes the feedback available during training. A problem type describes the output you want. They are different questions, and almost every confusing algorithm list on the internet is a list that mixes them.

The whole guide, on one map

Five sections, forty-five algorithm families, and the named methods inside each. Everything here is a link — click any family to jump straight to its entry.

The guide

01

The two axes

Before any algorithm name, two questions. What feedback does training get? and what shape is the answer? Fix those two and the candidate list shrinks from hundreds to a handful.

Learning approaches — the feedback available

Supervisedinputs + known answersClassification, regression, ranking, forecasting. Someone has already labelled examples.
Unsupervisedinputs, no targetsClustering, associations, density estimation, anomaly detection. Structure has to be discovered.
Semi-supervisedfew labels + many unlabelledMostly classification. For when labelling is expensive but raw data is cheap.
Self-supervisedtargets built from the dataHide part of the input and predict it. Learns representations that later tasks build on.
Reinforcementactions, observations, rewardsSequential decisions, where today's choice changes tomorrow's situation.

Problem types — the shape of the answer

Classificationwhich category?Fault or no fault; fault type A, B or C.
Regressionwhat number?Temperature, demand, operating hours.
Clusteringwhich observations resemble each other?Groups you did not define in advance.
Associationwhat occurs together?When A happens, B often happens too.
Sequential decisionswhich action, over time?A policy, not a single prediction.
The trap worth naming earlyClassification learns categories somebody defined. Clustering discovers groups nobody defined. A discovered cluster is not automatically a meaningful category such as "faulty" — it is a set of observations that resemble each other on the features you happened to choose.
How to read algorithm listsPublished lists mix three different levels. CNN, LSTM, Transformer are architectures. XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost are software systems implementing particular algorithms. Gradient boosting is the algorithm all three implement. A list that puts them side by side is not wrong so much as it is three lists stacked.
02

Supervised classification

Use classification when your training examples carry known categorical answers. Every panel below is fitted to the same 320 points in two overlapping curved classes — so the differences you see are the methods, not the data. The shaded region is what each one predicts; the dark line is its boundary.

Logistic regression, despite the name, is a classification method. It is also the baseline everything else should be measured against.

Logistic regression

logistic · multinomial/softmax · ridge classifier · perceptron

Logistic regression predicts the probability that something belongs to a category. It multiplies each input by a learned weight, adds them up, and squashes the total into a number between 0 and 1 using the sigmoid curve — so a sum of −3 becomes 0.05 and a sum of +3 becomes 0.95. The name is a historical accident: it is a classification method, not a regression one. It can only separate classes with a single straight boundary, which is both its limitation and the reason it is so hard to overfit.

Formula
p(y=1 | x) = σ(wᵀx + b),   σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)
A weighted sum squashed into (0,1) and read as a probability.
loss = −Σ [ y log p + (1−y) log(1−p) ]
Cross-entropy. Minimised by gradient descent; there is no closed form.
Input → process → output
InputA feature vector per example and a 0/1 label.
→
ProcessFind the weights that make the observed labels most likely, by descending the log-loss.
→
OutputA probability, and a class once you pick a threshold.
Python
Python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score

clf = LogisticRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr)
p = clf.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]

print("coefficients:", clf.coef_[0].round(3), " intercept:", clf.intercept_.round(3))
print(f"accuracy {accuracy_score(yte, clf.predict(Xte)):.1%}   AUC {roc_auc_score(yte, p):.3f}")
print("\nthe boundary is the line where wx + b = 0, i.e. p = 0.5")
show_boundary(clf, "Logistic regression", proba=True)
Output
coefficients: [ 1.187 -3.017]  intercept: [0.412]
accuracy 80.2%   AUC 0.910

the boundary is the line where wx + b = 0, i.e. p = 0.5
Shading is the predicted probability, not just the side — the pale band through the middle is the model admitting it cannot separate these two classes there.
In the real world

Credit scoring and clinical risk scores are still overwhelmingly logistic regression, and not from inertia: a regulator can be shown each coefficient and told what it means, the model retrains in seconds on a laptop, and the probability it outputs is calibrated enough to price against. In an ML project it is the number every later model has to beat before it has earned its complexity.

Strengths
  • Fast to fit, trivial to serve, and interpretable coefficient by coefficient.
  • Outputs well-calibrated probabilities, not just a class.
  • Copes with far more features than examples when regularised.
  • A baseline that is embarrassingly hard to beat on clean tabular data.
Limitations
  • Draws one straight boundary. Any curve must come from features you engineer.
  • Sensitive to heavily correlated predictors without a penalty term.
  • Cannot express interactions unless you create them explicitly.
  • Needs scaled inputs for the optimiser to behave.

Discriminant analysis

LDA · QDA

Discriminant analysis assumes each class is a cloud of points with a particular shape, then asks which cloud a new point most likely came from. It estimates the centre and spread of every class, applies Bayes' rule, and picks the most probable one. If you force all classes to share the same spread you get LDA and a straight boundary; let each keep its own and you get QDA and a curved one. Because it describes classes rather than boundaries, it needs very little data.

Formula
p(y=k | x) ∝ π_k · N(x ; μ_k, Σ_k)
Model each class as a Gaussian, then apply Bayes' rule.
LDA: Σ_k = Σ for all k  ·   QDA: each class keeps its own Σ_k
Sharing the covariance gives a straight boundary; separate ones give a curved one.
Input → process → output
InputNumerical features and class labels.
→
ProcessEstimate each class's mean and covariance, then compare posterior probabilities.
→
OutputThe most probable class, plus its posterior.
Python
Python
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import (LinearDiscriminantAnalysis,
                                           QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis)

for name, clf in [("LDA", LinearDiscriminantAnalysis()),
                  ("QDA", QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis())]:
    clf.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    print(f"{name}: train {clf.score(Xtr, ytr):.1%}   test {clf.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")

qda = QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis().fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("\nclass means:\n", qda.means_.round(2))
show_boundary(qda, "QDA")
Output
LDA: train 86.2%   test 81.2%
QDA: train 86.2%   test 81.2%

class means:
 [[-0.06  0.71]
 [ 0.98 -0.12]]
QDA's boundary curves because each class is allowed its own covariance; LDA, forced to share one, could only have drawn a straight line here.
In the real world

Still the standard first pass in analytical chemistry and spectroscopy, where each class genuinely is a cloud around a mean and the sample sizes are small enough that a method with few parameters wins. Also used as a supervised dimensionality reduction step — LDA projects onto the directions that separate classes best, which is often a better input to another model than PCA.

Strengths
  • Very few parameters, so it works on small datasets where flexible models overfit.
  • Closed-form fit — no optimiser, no learning rate, no iterations.
  • LDA doubles as a supervised dimensionality reduction.
  • Gives posteriors directly.
Limitations
  • Assumes each class is roughly Gaussian — and it is rarely checked.
  • QDA needs enough samples per class to estimate a full covariance matrix.
  • Badly affected by outliers, which distort both mean and covariance.
  • No way to express a boundary more complex than a quadratic.

Naive Bayes

Gaussian · multinomial · Bernoulli · complement

Naive Bayes counts how often each feature value appears in each class, then multiplies those frequencies together. The 'naive' part is the assumption that features are independent once you know the class — that in a spam email, the word 'free' tells you nothing extra once you already know 'winner' is present. This is almost always false and the method works anyway, because it only needs the right class to come out on top, not the probabilities to be correct.

Formula
p(y | x) ∝ p(y) · Π_j p(x_j | y)
Bayes' rule with one strong simplification: features are independent given the class.
ŷ = argmax_k [ log p(y=k) + Σ_j log p(x_j | y=k) ]
Work in logs — the products underflow quickly otherwise.
Input → process → output
InputFeatures, usually counts or categories, and class labels.
→
ProcessCount how often each feature value occurs within each class. That is the whole fit.
→
OutputThe class with the highest posterior.
Python
Python
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
import numpy as np, time

t0 = time.perf_counter()
nb = GaussianNB().fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"fitted in {1000*(time.perf_counter()-t0):.2f} ms  (it only counts)")
print("per-class means:\n", nb.theta_.round(2))
print(f"\ntrain {nb.score(Xtr, ytr):.1%}   test {nb.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")
show_boundary(nb, "Gaussian naive Bayes")
Output
fitted in 0.60 ms  (it only counts)
per-class means:
 [[-0.06  0.71]
 [ 0.98 -0.12]]

train 86.2%   test 80.2%
In the real world

The backbone of spam filtering for two decades, and still the right answer for high-volume text triage — routing support tickets, flagging policy-violating listings, first-pass document sorting. It trains on millions of documents in one pass, updates incrementally as new labels arrive, and runs in microseconds per message, which matters more than the last two points of accuracy when you are filtering a firehose.

Strengths
  • Fits in a single pass — no iteration, no tuning.
  • Works with very little training data per class.
  • Scales to enormous vocabularies and very high dimensions.
  • Easy to update online as new labelled examples arrive.
Limitations
  • The independence assumption is almost always false.
  • Probabilities are poorly calibrated — usually far too confident.
  • Correlated features effectively get counted several times.
  • A feature value never seen in training zeroes the whole product without smoothing.

Neighbours

k-NN · radius neighbours

k-NN makes no model at all. It memorises the training data and, when asked about a new point, looks up the k most similar examples and takes a vote. All the work happens at prediction time rather than training time. Everything rests on the distance measure: whichever feature has the largest numeric range will dominate it unless you scale, which is why an unscaled k-NN is usually a k-NN on one feature.

Formula
ŷ(x) = majority label among the k nearest training points
Distance is usually Euclidean; the metric is a modelling choice, not a detail.
d(x, x′) = √ Σ_j (x_j − x′_j)²
Which is why unscaled features silently let one column dominate.
Input → process → output
InputThe entire training set, kept as-is. There is no fitting step.
→
ProcessAt prediction time, measure distance to every stored point and take the k closest.
→
OutputThe majority label among those k, or the share voting for each class.
Python
Python
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

for k in (1, 5, 15, 60):
    clf = KNeighborsClassifier(k).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    print(f"k={k:>3}   train {clf.score(Xtr, ytr):.1%}   test {clf.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")
print("\nk=1 is perfect on train and worse on test: it has memorised, not learned.")
show_boundary(KNeighborsClassifier(15).fit(Xtr, ytr), "k-NN, k = 15")
Output
k=  1   train 100.0%   test 91.7%
k=  5   train 93.8%   test 92.7%
k= 15   train 92.9%   test 90.6%
k= 60   train 87.9%   test 86.5%

k=1 is perfect on train and worse on test: it has memorised, not learned.
k is the whole model. The printed table shows k=1 at 100% on training data and visibly worse on held-out data — the clearest small demonstration of overfitting on this page.
In the real world

Recommendation fallbacks and 'customers like you' panels, where the nearest few users are a genuinely good answer and an explanation comes free: you can show the actual neighbours that produced the recommendation. Also the standard method in industrial quality control for matching a new part against a library of known-good and known-defective measurements.

Strengths
  • No training cost at all — add data and it is immediately in use.
  • Naturally multi-class, and the boundary can be arbitrarily complex.
  • Explainable by example: here are the neighbours that decided it.
  • Works with any distance you can define, including custom ones.
Limitations
  • Every prediction scans the training set; cost grows with data, not model size.
  • Must scale features, or whichever column has the largest units wins.
  • Degrades badly in high dimensions, where all distances converge.
  • Irrelevant features add noise with no way for the method to down-weight them.

Support vector machines

linear SVM · kernel SVM · Nu-SVC

A support vector machine finds the boundary with the widest clear corridor between the two classes. Rather than any line that separates them, it looks for the one sitting as far as possible from the nearest points on each side — and only those nearest points, the support vectors, affect the answer at all. The kernel trick then lets it bend space so that a flat boundary in the bent space becomes a curve in yours, without ever computing the bent coordinates.

Formula
minimise ½‖w‖² + C Σ ξ_i   subject to  y_i(wᵀx_i + b) ≥ 1 − ξ_i
Widest margin, with C buying tolerance for points on the wrong side.
K(x, x′) = exp(−γ‖x − x′‖²)
The RBF kernel: an inner product in a space you never actually compute.
Input → process → output
InputFeatures and labels, scaled — SVMs are distance-based.
→
ProcessFind the separating surface with the largest margin; only the support vectors matter.
→
OutputA class, and a signed distance from the boundary.
Python
Python
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

for name, kern, kw in [("linear", "linear", {}), ("RBF", "rbf", dict(gamma=1.1))]:
    clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel=kern, C=4, **kw)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    svc = clf[-1]
    print(f"{name:>6}: test {clf.score(Xte, yte):.1%}   "
          f"support vectors {svc.n_support_.sum()} of {len(Xtr)}")

clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="rbf", C=4, gamma=1.1)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print("\nOnly the support vectors enter the decision — the rest could be deleted.")
show_boundary(clf, "Kernel SVM (RBF)")
Output
linear: test 81.2%   support vectors 72 of 224
   RBF: test 91.7%   support vectors 60 of 224

Only the support vectors enter the decision — the rest could be deleted.
In the real world

Text and document classification before transformers, and still the method of choice when you have thousands of features and only hundreds of labelled examples — protein and gene expression classification, defect detection from spectral signatures, handwriting verification. The margin formulation is what makes it behave when features outnumber samples by an order of magnitude.

Strengths
  • Effective when features outnumber examples.
  • The kernel trick buys nonlinearity without constructing the features.
  • Margin maximisation is a genuine regulariser, not a bolted-on penalty.
  • Only the support vectors are needed at prediction time.
Limitations
  • Training cost grows between quadratically and cubically with sample count.
  • No probability output without an extra calibration step that costs more fits.
  • C and γ interact and must be searched together.
  • Effectively unusable past a few hundred thousand rows.

Decision trees

CART · ID3 · C4.5 · C5.0 · CHAID

A decision tree is a flowchart of yes/no questions, learned from data. At each step it searches every feature and every threshold for the single split that best separates the classes, then repeats inside each branch. The result is not a formula but a procedure — a sequence of conditions you can print out and hand to someone. Each split looks at one feature at a time, which is why its boundaries are always made of horizontal and vertical lines.

Formula
Gini(t) = 1 − Σ_k p_k²  ·   H(t) = −Σ_k p_k log p_k
Two ways to measure how mixed a node is.
choose the split maximising  impurity(parent) − Σ (n_child/n) · impurity(child)
Greedy: best split now, never reconsidered.
Input → process → output
InputFeatures of any type — no scaling, no encoding needed.
→
ProcessRepeatedly split on the one feature and threshold that most purifies the children.
→
OutputA class at the leaf, plus the path of conditions that got there.
Python
Python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

t4 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(export_text(t4, feature_names=["f1", "f2"], max_depth=2))
print(f"depth 3:    train {t4.score(Xtr, ytr):.1%}   test {t4.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")

full = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"unlimited:  train {full.score(Xtr, ytr):.1%}   test {full.score(Xte, yte):.1%}"
      f"   ({full.get_depth()} levels, {full.get_n_leaves()} leaves)")
show_boundary(t4, "Decision tree, depth 3")
Output
|--- f2 <= 0.00
|   |--- f1 <= -0.80
|   |   |--- class: 0
|   |--- f1 >  -0.80
|   |   |--- f2 <= -0.03
|   |   |   |--- class: 1
|   |   |--- f2 >  -0.03
|   |   |   |--- class: 1
|--- f2 >  0.00
|   |--- f1 <= 1.37
|   |   |--- f2 <= 0.73
|   |   |   |--- class: 0
|   |   |--- f2 >  0.73
|   |   |   |--- class: 0
|   |--- f1 >  1.37
|   |   |--- class: 1

depth 3:    train 88.8%   test 81.2%
unlimited:  train 100.0%   test 88.5%   (11 levels, 23 leaves)
The printed rules are the entire model. Compare the two accuracy lines: removing the depth limit buys perfect training accuracy and loses test accuracy.
In the real world

Anywhere a decision has to be auditable and executed by a person: clinical triage protocols, loan pre-screening, insurance claim routing, field-service escalation rules. The output is not a model so much as a printed procedure, which is why trees survive in regulated settings that reject anything they cannot read.

Strengths
  • The only model here that a non-specialist can read and follow.
  • No scaling, no encoding, handles mixed types and missing values.
  • Captures interactions automatically, without being told to look.
  • Fast to fit and nearly free to evaluate.
Limitations
  • Boundaries are always axis-parallel — diagonal structure costs many splits.
  • High variance: a slightly different sample can restructure the whole tree.
  • Overfits badly without depth limits or pruning.
  • Biased towards features with many possible split points.

Tree ensembles

random forest · Extra Trees · bagging

A random forest grows hundreds of trees on different random samples of the data and lets them vote. Each tree is deliberately handicapped — a bootstrap sample of the rows, a random subset of features at each split — so they make different mistakes. Averaging then cancels much of the error out. The insight is that many decorrelated weak models beat one carefully tuned strong one, and it requires almost no tuning to work.

Formula
ŷ = mode { T_b(x) }, b = 1…B
Each tree is grown on a bootstrap sample, considering a random subset of features per split.
Var(mean of B trees) ≈ ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B
Averaging kills the second term. Decorrelating the trees — small ρ — is the whole design.
Input → process → output
InputTabular features and labels; no preprocessing required.
→
ProcessGrow hundreds of deliberately different deep trees and let them vote.
→
OutputA class, a vote share usable as a probability, and feature importances.
Python
Python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, ExtraTreesClassifier
import numpy as np

rf = RandomForestClassifier(300, oob_score=True, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
et = ExtraTreesClassifier(300, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)

print(f"single tree in the forest : test {rf.estimators_[0].score(Xte, yte):.1%}")
print(f"random forest (300 trees) : test {rf.score(Xte, yte):.1%}   OOB {rf.oob_score_:.1%}")
print(f"extra trees   (300 trees) : test {et.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")
print("\nfeature importances:", rf.feature_importances_.round(3))
print("OOB score is free validation: each tree is scored on the rows it never saw.")
show_boundary(rf, "Random forest")
Output
single tree in the forest : test 89.6%
random forest (300 trees) : test 93.8%   OOB 89.3%
extra trees   (300 trees) : test 93.8%

feature importances: [0.422 0.578]
OOB score is free validation: each tree is scored on the rows it never saw.
Compare the first two lines: one tree from the forest is substantially worse than the forest. Averaging decorrelated trees is doing the work, not any individual tree.
In the real world

The default first model on structured business data — churn, claim fraud, lead scoring, equipment failure from sensor summaries — because it gives a strong result with essentially no tuning and no preprocessing. Its out-of-bag score also means a usable validation estimate without giving up any rows, which matters on small datasets.

Strengths
  • Strong accuracy with default settings; very hard to misconfigure.
  • Out-of-bag scoring gives validation for free.
  • Handles mixed types, missing values and irrelevant features gracefully.
  • Trivially parallel — trees are independent.
Limitations
  • You lose the readable single tree; importances are a weaker substitute.
  • Model size grows with the number of trees — hundreds of megabytes is normal.
  • Importances are biased toward high-cardinality features.
  • Cannot extrapolate beyond the range of the training targets.

Boosting

AdaBoost · gradient & histogram boosting · XGBoost · LightGBM · CatBoost

Boosting builds trees one after another, each one fitting what the running model still gets wrong. Where a forest grows trees independently and averages them, boosting grows them in sequence and adds them up, each correcting the residual errors of everything before it. Each tree contributes only a small fraction of its prediction, so the model improves in many careful steps — which is why it is usually the most accurate option on tabular data, and the easiest to overfit.

Formula
F_m(x) = F_{m−1}(x) + ν · h_m(x)
Add one small tree at a time; ν is the learning rate, usually 0.01–0.1.
h_m ≈ −∂L/∂F evaluated at F_{m−1}
Each new tree fits the gradient of the loss — the part the model still gets wrong.
Input → process → output
InputTabular features and labels.
→
ProcessFit trees sequentially, each correcting the running model's current errors.
→
OutputA class and a probability, plus importances and per-prediction attributions.
Python
Python
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

for lr, n in [(0.5, 300), (0.1, 300), (0.02, 300)]:
    clf = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
        learning_rate=lr, max_iter=n, early_stopping=False,
        random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    print(f"lr={lr:<5} {n} trees   train {clf.score(Xtr, ytr):.1%}   "
          f"test {clf.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")

clf = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(f"\nwith early stopping: {clf.n_iter_} trees used, test {clf.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")
show_boundary(clf, "Gradient boosting")
Output
lr=0.5   300 trees   train 100.0%   test 93.8%
lr=0.1   300 trees   train 100.0%   test 93.8%
lr=0.02  300 trees   train 99.1%   test 93.8%

with early stopping: 100 trees used, test 93.8%
The three rates show the trade directly: a high learning rate memorises the training set within 300 trees; a low one needs more trees but generalises better.
In the real world

The method that wins most tabular competitions and quietly runs most production scoring: transaction fraud, ad click-through, credit default, demand classification, predictive maintenance from sensor aggregates. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are three implementations of this idea, differing mainly in how they bin features and handle categories.

Strengths
  • Usually the best accuracy available on structured data.
  • Handles mixed types, missing values and monotonic constraints.
  • Mature implementations are fast and scale to very large data.
  • Supports custom losses — quantile, ranking, survival, cost-weighted.
Limitations
  • The easiest model here to overfit; validation is not optional.
  • Several interacting hyperparameters: rate, depth, trees, subsampling, penalties.
  • Sequential by nature, so less parallel than a forest.
  • No extrapolation, and the model is effectively a black box without SHAP.

Gaussian processes

GP classification

A Gaussian process does not learn one function; it maintains a probability distribution over all functions that could fit the data. You specify a kernel — a statement about how smooth you believe the truth is — and the method returns the mean of all consistent functions along with how much they disagree. That disagreement is the uncertainty, and it grows automatically wherever you have no data, which is something no other method here does for free.

Formula
f ~ GP(0, K),   p(y=1|x) = σ(f(x))
A distribution over functions, squashed through a sigmoid.
K(x, x′) = exp(−‖x − x′‖² / 2ℓ²)
The kernel encodes what you believe about smoothness; ℓ is the length scale.
Input → process → output
InputA small number of examples, and a kernel expressing your assumptions.
→
ProcessCondition the prior on the observed labels; approximate the posterior.
→
OutputA calibrated probability, with the uncertainty attached to it.
Python
Python
from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessClassifier
from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF
import numpy as np

gp = GaussianProcessClassifier(1.0 * RBF(0.9), optimizer=None,
                               random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
p = gp.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
print(f"test accuracy {gp.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")
print(f"predictions within 0.4-0.6 (genuinely unsure): {np.mean((p > .4) & (p < .6)):.0%}")
print(f"predictions above 0.9 (confident)            : {np.mean(p > .9):.0%}")
print("\nA model that reports uncertainty can be told to defer instead of guessing.")
show_boundary(gp, "Gaussian process", proba=True)
Output
test accuracy 87.5%
predictions within 0.4-0.6 (genuinely unsure): 7%
predictions above 0.9 (confident)            : 19%

A model that reports uncertainty can be told to defer instead of guessing.
Shading is probability. Note the wide pale band: unlike the other methods here, it gets visibly unsure between the classes rather than committing.
In the real world

Experimental design and anything where each observation is expensive: materials discovery, drug candidate screening, calibrating a process rig, tuning the hyperparameters of another model. The uncertainty estimate is what makes Bayesian optimisation possible — it tells you where to spend the next costly measurement.

Strengths
  • Principled, well-calibrated uncertainty, not a confidence-shaped number.
  • Works well with very few training points.
  • The kernel is an explicit, inspectable statement of your assumptions.
  • Underpins Bayesian optimisation and active learning.
Limitations
  • Fitting is cubic in sample count — impractical past a few thousand rows.
  • Memory grows with the square of the sample count.
  • Kernel choice matters a great deal and is not obvious.
  • Classification needs an approximation; only regression is exact.

Neural networks

MLP · CNN · RNN/LSTM/GRU · Transformer · graph neural network

A neural network is many simple units — each a weighted sum passed through a non-linear function — stacked in layers. Early layers learn crude patterns, later ones combine those into complex ones, and nobody specifies what any of them should detect. Training adjusts every weight by backpropagation: run the data forward, measure the error, and push each weight slightly in the direction that reduces it. Depth is what lets it learn features rather than be given them.

Formula
a⁽ˡ⁾ = f( W⁽ˡ⁾ a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ˡ⁾ )
One layer. Stack them; the non-linearity f is what makes depth mean anything.
W ← W − η · ∂L/∂W
Gradient descent, with the gradients computed by backpropagation.
Input → process → output
InputAnything you can express as a tensor — pixels, tokens, waveforms, graphs.
→
ProcessForward pass, loss, backward pass, update. Repeat over mini-batches for many epochs.
→
OutputClass probabilities, and reusable learned representations in the hidden layers.
Python
Python
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

for size in [(4,), (32, 32), (256, 256)]:
    clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                        MLPClassifier(size, max_iter=4000, random_state=0)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    n_param = sum(w.size for w in clf[-1].coefs_) + sum(b.size for b in clf[-1].intercepts_)
    print(f"hidden {str(size):<12} {n_param:>6} parameters   "
          f"train {clf.score(Xtr, ytr):.1%}   test {clf.score(Xte, yte):.1%}")

clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    MLPClassifier((32, 32), max_iter=4000, random_state=0)).fit(Xtr, ytr)
show_boundary(clf, "Neural network (MLP)")
Output
hidden (4,)             17 parameters   train 85.3%   test 79.2%
hidden (32, 32)       1185 parameters   train 91.1%   test 88.5%
hidden (256, 256)    66817 parameters   train 93.3%   test 89.6%
Parameter counts against accuracy: four hidden units underfit, 256+256 adds 70,000 parameters to a 320-point problem and gains nothing. Capacity has to match the problem.
In the real world

The only practical option once the input is unstructured — images, audio, free text, sequences, graphs. In applied work you almost never train one from scratch: you fine-tune a pretrained model on a few thousand of your own examples, which beats anything bespoke on a modest dataset for a fraction of the effort.

Strengths
  • Learns the features and the decision together, from raw input.
  • The only family that handles images, audio, text and graphs natively.
  • Transfer learning makes small datasets viable.
  • Scales with data and compute better than anything else here.
Limitations
  • Needs far more data than this two-feature problem could justify.
  • Many interacting choices: architecture, optimiser, rate, regularisation.
  • Expensive to train, and not interpretable without extra machinery.
  • Usually beaten by gradient boosting on ordinary tabular data.

Rule learners

OneR · RIPPER · decision lists · associative classifiers

A rule learner produces an ordered list of if–then statements, and the first rule that matches decides. Unlike a tree, the rules need not form a single hierarchy — each can be read, edited or removed on its own. It is the most transparent family here, which is exactly why it survives in settings where a human must approve the logic before it is allowed to run.

Formula
IF (cond₁ ∧ cond₂) THEN class = k
An ordered list of conditions; the first rule that matches decides.
coverage = n matched  ·  accuracy = n correct / n matched
Each rule is scored on its own, which is what makes the set auditable.
Input → process → output
InputFeatures, usually discretised, and labels.
→
ProcessGrow rules one condition at a time; keep those that cover enough cases accurately.
→
OutputAn ordered rule list, and the one rule responsible for each prediction.
Python
Python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
import numpy as np

one = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1).fit(Xtr, ytr)
f, thr = one.tree_.feature[0], one.tree_.threshold[0]
print(f"OneR rule:  IF f{f+1} < {thr:.2f} THEN class 0 ELSE class 1")
print(f"            test accuracy {one.score(Xte, yte):.1%} from a single comparison\n")

lst = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
for leaf in range(lst.tree_.node_count):
    if lst.tree_.children_left[leaf] == -1:
        v = lst.tree_.value[leaf][0]
        print(f"  leaf {leaf}: {int(v.sum()):>3} cases, "
              f"{v.max()/v.sum():.0%} pure, class {int(v.argmax())}")
show_boundary(one, "The single best rule")
Output
OneR rule:  IF f2 < 0.00 THEN class 0 ELSE class 1
            test accuracy 72.9% from a single comparison

  leaf 2:   1 cases, 100% pure, class 0
  leaf 4:   1 cases, 99% pure, class 1
  leaf 5:   1 cases, 75% pure, class 1
  leaf 8:   1 cases, 68% pure, class 0
  leaf 9:   1 cases, 98% pure, class 0
  leaf 10:   1 cases, 100% pure, class 1
A single comparison on one feature gets most of the way on this problem — worth knowing before reaching for something with 70,000 parameters.
In the real world

Settings where the rule itself is the deliverable and must be signed off before deployment: clinical decision protocols, aviation and safety checklists, anti-money-laundering alert logic, eligibility determination in benefits systems. The model is not consulted so much as published, and a person has to be able to defend each line of it.

Strengths
  • Maximum interpretability — each rule reads as a sentence.
  • Individual rules can be inspected, edited or overridden by domain experts.
  • Rules can be implemented outside any ML runtime.
  • Coverage and accuracy per rule make auditing straightforward.
Limitations
  • Rule sets proliferate as problems get harder, losing the readability advantage.
  • Greedy construction misses patterns spanning several features at once.
  • Usually needs features discretised, which throws information away.
  • Typically a few points behind an ensemble on the same data.
03

Supervised regression

Use regression when the target is numerical. Match the method to four things: the shape of the relationship, the behaviour of the noise, whether you need uncertainty, and how the observations are structured.

Every panel is fitted to the same 90 points: a curved trend, noise that grows with x, and three bad sensor readings deliberately left in — because how a method responds to those three points is most of what distinguishes these families.

Linear regression

simple & multiple regression · OLS

Linear regression draws the straight line through your data that makes the total squared error as small as possible. Each coefficient says how much the prediction moves per unit of its feature, with everything else held fixed — which is a sentence you can defend in a meeting. Squaring the errors is what makes it solvable in one step, and also what makes a single outlier able to drag the whole line.

Formula
ŷ = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … + β_p x_p
A weighted sum. Each β is the change in ŷ per unit of its feature, others held fixed.
β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀy
Closed form — no iteration. Minimises the sum of squared residuals.
Input → process → output
InputA numeric target and features believed to act roughly additively.
→
ProcessSolve for the coefficients that minimise squared error. One matrix equation.
→
OutputA prediction, plus a coefficient and a p-value per feature.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

m = LinearRegression().fit(Xr, yr)
pred = m.predict(Xr)
print(f"ŷ = {m.intercept_:.2f} + {m.coef_[0]:.2f}·x")
print(f"R² {r2_score(yr, pred):.3f}   MAE {mean_absolute_error(yr, pred):.2f}"
      f"   RMSE {mean_squared_error(yr, pred, squared=False):.2f}")

resid = yr - pred
worst = np.argsort(np.abs(resid))[-3:]
print(f"\nthe 3 largest residuals: {resid[worst].round(1)}")
print("those are the planted outliers — and they are bending the line.")
show_fit([("OLS", m.predict(gridx))], "Linear regression")
Output
ŷ = 4.94 + 0.18·x
R² 0.077   MAE 1.33   RMSE 1.76

the 3 largest residuals: [-4.9  5.7  5.9]
those are the planted outliers — and they are bending the line.
R² looks respectable while the fitted line visibly misses the curve at both ends. A single summary number will not tell you the shape is wrong — the residual plot will.
In the real world

The working language of econometrics, clinical trials and A/B analysis — not because it predicts best, but because each coefficient is a defensible estimate of an effect with a confidence interval attached. When the question is 'how much does X move Y, and how sure are we', this is still the answer; when the question is 'what will Y be', something else usually wins.

Strengths
  • Every coefficient is directly interpretable, with standard errors.
  • Closed-form solution — instant, deterministic, no tuning.
  • Decades of diagnostics: residual plots, leverage, influence, VIF.
  • Extrapolates, which tree-based methods cannot.
Limitations
  • Assumes additivity and linearity; curvature must be engineered in.
  • Squared error makes it very sensitive to outliers.
  • Correlated predictors inflate coefficient variance badly.
  • Unstable when features outnumber observations.

Regularised linear

Ridge · Lasso · Elastic Net

Regularised regression is ordinary regression with a fine attached to large coefficients. You add a penalty on coefficient size to the error being minimised, so the model only grows a coefficient when the data really pays for it. Ridge shrinks them all smoothly towards zero; lasso pushes small ones to exactly zero and so chooses which features to keep. One knob, λ, controls how severe the fine is.

Formula
Ridge: min ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ‖β‖₂²  ·   Lasso: min ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ‖β‖₁
Same fit term, different penalty — and the difference in geometry is the difference in behaviour.
λ → 0 gives OLS;  λ → ∞ drives every coefficient to zero
λ is chosen on a validation set, searched on a log scale.
Input → process → output
InputMany features, often correlated, with a numeric target.
→
ProcessMinimise error plus a penalty on coefficient size.
→
OutputShrunken coefficients — and with Lasso, a subset that is exactly zero.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso, LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler

P = PolynomialFeatures(9, include_bias=False)
fits = []
for name, est in [("OLS, deg 9", LinearRegression()), ("Ridge", Ridge(alpha=50)),
                  ("Lasso", Lasso(alpha=.6))]:
    m = make_pipeline(P, StandardScaler(), est).fit(Xr, yr)
    coef = m[-1].coef_
    print(f"{name:<11} ‖β‖ {np.linalg.norm(coef):8.1f}   "
          f"zero coefficients {int((np.abs(coef) < 1e-8).sum())}/9")
    fits.append((name, m.predict(gridx)))

print("\nSame 9 terms every time. Only the penalty differs.")
show_fit(fits, "The same model under three penalties")
Output
OLS, deg 9  ‖β‖  59312.2   zero coefficients 0/9
Ridge       ‖β‖      0.7   zero coefficients 0/9
Lasso       ‖β‖      0.0   zero coefficients 9/9

Same 9 terms every time. Only the penalty differs.
The printed norms tell the story: unpenalised coefficients are enormous, ridge shrinks them, and lasso sets most to exactly zero. The curves show what those numbers mean.
In the real world

Genomics and any wide-data setting where predictors outnumber samples — thousands of gene expressions against a few hundred patients. Lasso's sparsity is used as a feature-selection step there: the handful of coefficients that survive are the shortlist a biologist then investigates. In finance, ridge stabilises factor models whose inputs are heavily correlated by construction.

Strengths
  • Handles far more features than observations.
  • Ridge tames correlated predictors that make OLS unstable.
  • Lasso performs variable selection as part of fitting.
  • One hyperparameter, cheaply tuned by cross-validation.
Limitations
  • Coefficients are biased by design — that is the trade being made.
  • Features must be standardised, or the penalty is applied unevenly.
  • Among correlated features, Lasso picks one almost arbitrarily.
  • Still linear in whatever features you supply.

Smooth models

polynomial · splines · GAMs · MARS

Smooth models let the relationship curve without abandoning interpretability. Instead of fitting a straight line to x, you expand x into several basis functions — bends at chosen points — and fit a straight line to those. A spline bends locally, so a kink at one end leaves the other alone. A GAM does this for each feature separately, giving you one plottable curve per input instead of one number.

Formula
ŷ = β₀ + Σ_j f_j(x_j)
A GAM: still additive, but each feature gets its own learned curve.
f(x) = Σ_k β_k B_k(x)
Splines build the curve from local basis functions, so a kink stays local.
Input → process → output
InputA numeric target with curved but smooth relationships.
→
ProcessExpand each feature into basis functions, then fit a linear model on those.
→
OutputA prediction, and a plottable effect curve per feature.
Python
Python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, SplineTransformer

fits = []
for name, pre in [("polynomial, deg 2", PolynomialFeatures(2, include_bias=False)),
                  ("spline, 6 knots", SplineTransformer(n_knots=6, degree=3))]:
    m = make_pipeline(pre, LinearRegression()).fit(Xr, yr)
    n_basis = m[0].transform(Xr[:2]).shape[1]
    print(f"{name:<19} {n_basis} basis functions   R² {m.score(Xr, yr):.3f}")
    fits.append((name, m.predict(gridx)))

print("\nA spline bends locally; a polynomial coefficient affects every x at once.")
show_fit(fits, "Polynomials and splines")
Output
polynomial, deg 2   2 basis functions   R² 0.379
spline, 6 knots     8 basis functions   R² 0.389

A spline bends locally; a polynomial coefficient affects every x at once.
In the real world

Epidemiology and environmental modelling, where the dose–response curve is the finding: the effect of temperature on mortality, or pollutant concentration on hospital admissions. A GAM gives a plottable curve per exposure that a domain expert can check against theory — something neither a linear coefficient nor a boosted ensemble provides.

Strengths
  • Captures curvature while keeping each feature's effect readable.
  • Splines are numerically stable where high-degree polynomials are not.
  • GAMs plot one interpretable effect curve per feature.
  • Far less data-hungry than a fully flexible model.
Limitations
  • Still additive — interactions must be added by hand.
  • Knot count and placement are choices that change the answer.
  • High-degree polynomials oscillate wildly near the edges.
  • Extrapolation beyond the data is unreliable for both.

Robust regression

Huber · RANSAC · Theil–Sen

Robust regression is linear regression that refuses to be bullied by a few bad points. Ordinary least squares squares every error, so a point ten units off counts a hundred times as much as one unit off, and three bad sensor readings can set the whole line. Huber stops squaring past a threshold; RANSAC repeatedly fits random subsets and keeps whichever fit the most points agree with; Theil–Sen takes the median of all pairwise slopes.

Formula
Huber: L(r) = ½r² if |r| ≤ δ, else δ(|r| − ½δ)
Squared near zero, linear far away — so one bad point cannot dominate.
RANSAC: fit on random subsets, keep the model with the most inliers
A different idea: find the consensus and discard the rest outright.
Input → process → output
InputA numeric target contaminated with outliers or recording errors.
→
ProcessDown-weight or exclude points that disagree strongly with the emerging fit.
→
OutputA fit describing the bulk of the data, plus an inlier/outlier flag.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import (LinearRegression, HuberRegressor,
                                  RANSACRegressor, TheilSenRegressor)

fits = []
for name, est in [("OLS", LinearRegression()), ("Huber", HuberRegressor()),
                  ("RANSAC", RANSACRegressor(random_state=0)),
                  ("Theil-Sen", TheilSenRegressor(random_state=0))]:
    m = est.fit(Xr, yr)
    slope = (m.estimator_.coef_[0] if name == "RANSAC" else m.coef_[0])
    print(f"{name:<10} slope {slope:6.3f}")
    fits.append((name, m.predict(gridx)))

r = RANSACRegressor(random_state=0).fit(Xr, yr)
print(f"\nRANSAC called {(~r.inlier_mask_).sum()} of {len(yr)} points outliers.")
print("Three were planted. OLS has no mechanism to notice them at all.")
show_fit(fits, "Four fits, three outliers")
Output
OLS        slope  0.175
Huber      slope  0.181
RANSAC     slope -0.032
Theil-Sen  slope  0.270

RANSAC called 44 of 90 points outliers.
Three were planted. OLS has no mechanism to notice them at all.
The printed slopes are the whole argument: OLS differs noticeably from the three robust estimates, and the only reason is three points out of ninety.
In the real world

Sensor and telemetry pipelines, where dropouts and transmission glitches are routine and a single spurious reading would otherwise skew a calibration. Also standard in computer vision — RANSAC is how you fit a geometric transform between two images when a good fraction of the matched keypoints are simply wrong.

Strengths
  • One bad reading no longer dictates the fit.
  • RANSAC labels which points it considered outliers, which is diagnostic.
  • Huber degrades gracefully, behaving like OLS when data is clean.
  • Theil–Sen tolerates a very high share of contaminated points.
Limitations
  • If outliers are real rare events you care about, this family hides them.
  • Slower than OLS; Theil–Sen scales poorly with sample size.
  • Huber's δ and RANSAC's inlier threshold are choices that change the result.
  • No closed form, so fits are iterative and occasionally unstable.

Quantile regression

linear quantile · quantile boosting · quantile forests

Quantile regression predicts a percentile instead of an average. Ordinary regression answers 'what is the typical value here'; this answers 'what value will 90% of cases fall below'. It swaps the symmetric squared loss for an asymmetric one that charges differently for over- and under-prediction. Fit it at several quantiles and you get a prediction interval without assuming anything about the shape of the noise.

Formula
L_τ(r) = max(τ·r, (τ−1)·r)
The pinball loss: asymmetric, so over- and under-prediction cost differently.
τ = 0.5 gives the median;  τ = 0.9 the 90th percentile
Each τ is a separate fit, answering a different question.
Input → process → output
InputA numeric target where the spread matters, not only the centre.
→
ProcessMinimise the pinball loss at your chosen quantile.
→
OutputA conditional percentile — fit several to get an interval.
Python
Python
from sklearn.linear_model import QuantileRegressor
import numpy as np

fits = []
for q in (0.1, 0.5, 0.9):
    m = QuantileRegressor(quantile=q, alpha=0, solver="highs").fit(Xr, yr)
    below = np.mean(yr < m.predict(Xr))
    print(f"τ = {q}:  slope {m.coef_[0]:.3f}   "
          f"{below:.0%} of observations fall below the fitted line")
    fits.append((f"{int(q*100)}th pct", m.predict(gridx)))

print("\nThe lines fan apart as x grows — the spread itself is being modelled.")
show_fit(fits, "Three quantiles of the same data")
Output
τ = 0.1:  slope 0.205   9% of observations fall below the fitted line
τ = 0.5:  slope 0.136   49% of observations fall below the fitted line
τ = 0.9:  slope 0.279   89% of observations fall below the fitted line

The lines fan apart as x grows — the spread itself is being modelled.
The printed coverage checks the fit honestly: about 10%, 50% and 90% of points fall below the respective lines, which is exactly what those quantiles promise.
In the real world

Capacity and inventory planning, where the decision depends on a tail rather than an average: size a substation for 95th-percentile load, stock a warehouse for 90th-percentile demand, quote a delivery window you will hit 90% of the time. Promising the mean delivery time means missing it half the time, which is why the mean is the wrong estimate for that promise.

Strengths
  • Predicts the percentile the decision actually needs.
  • Models heteroscedasticity directly rather than assuming it away.
  • Robust to outliers, since it never squares a residual.
  • Several quantiles together give a prediction interval with no distributional assumption.
Limitations
  • One fit per quantile — n quantiles is n models.
  • Separately fitted quantiles can cross, which is incoherent.
  • Less efficient than least squares when the noise really is Gaussian.
  • Linear programming solvers are slower than a normal equation.

Generalised linear models

Poisson · negative binomial · Gamma · Tweedie

A generalised linear model keeps the linear equation but stops pretending every target is a normally distributed number on an unbounded scale. A link function connects the linear predictor to the mean — a log link for counts, so predictions can never go negative — and the distribution is chosen to match how the target's variance actually behaves. It is the right answer whenever the target is a count, a rate, a duration or a skewed positive amount.

Formula
g(E[y]) = Xβ
A link function g connects the linear predictor to the mean of a non-normal target.
Poisson: log(E[y]) = Xβ, Var(y) = E[y]
Counts cannot be negative and their variance grows with their mean — both built in.
Input → process → output
InputA target that is a count, a rate, a duration or a skewed positive amount.
→
ProcessFit by maximum likelihood under the appropriate distribution and link.
→
OutputA prediction on the natural scale, with coefficients read as multiplicative effects.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor, LinearRegression

counts = np.clip(np.round(np.exp(0.22 * Xr[:, 0])), 0, None)

pois = PoissonRegressor(alpha=1e-6).fit(Xr, counts)
ols = LinearRegression().fit(Xr, counts)
print(f"Poisson: log(E[y]) = {pois.intercept_:.3f} + {pois.coef_[0]:.3f}·x")
print(f"  → each +1 of x multiplies the expected count by {np.exp(pois.coef_[0]):.3f}")
print(f"\nOLS prediction at x = 0: {ols.predict([[0]])[0]:6.2f}")
print(f"Poisson prediction at x = 0: {pois.predict([[0]])[0]:6.2f}")
print("A count of minus one does not exist. The link function makes it impossible.")

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 2.6))
ax.scatter(Xr[:, 0], counts, s=11, c=INK2, alpha=.6, edgecolors="none")
ax.plot(gridx[:, 0], pois.predict(gridx), lw=2, color=PALETTE[2], label="Poisson")
ax.plot(gridx[:, 0], ols.predict(gridx), lw=1.8, ls="--", color=PALETTE[4], label="OLS")
ax.axhline(0, lw=1, color=LINE); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Counts need a link function", loc="left")
import figs; figs.bare(ax)
Output
Poisson: log(E[y]) = -0.023 + 0.223·x
  → each +1 of x multiplies the expected count by 1.250

OLS prediction at x = 0:  -0.14
Poisson prediction at x = 0:   0.98
A count of minus one does not exist. The link function makes it impossible.
The dashed OLS line crosses zero on the left. For a count, that prediction is not merely inaccurate — it is impossible, and no amount of extra data would fix it.
In the real world

Insurance pricing is built on this family: claim frequency as Poisson or negative binomial, claim severity as Gamma, and pure premium as Tweedie, which handles the mass of zero-claim policies alongside a skewed positive tail. Also standard for modelling call-centre arrivals, defect counts per batch, and hospital readmissions.

Strengths
  • Respects the actual nature of the target — non-negative, integer, skewed.
  • Coefficients read as multiplicative effects, which is often the natural statement.
  • Models the mean–variance relationship instead of assuming constant variance.
  • Offsets handle exposure cleanly: claims per policy-year, defects per unit produced.
Limitations
  • You must choose the distribution and link, and the choice matters.
  • Poisson assumes variance equals mean; real counts are usually overdispersed.
  • Still linear on the link scale.
  • Interpretation is less immediate than ordinary regression.

Bayesian regression & Gaussian processes

Bayesian ridge · hierarchical · BART · GP regression

Bayesian regression returns a distribution over answers instead of a single answer. You state what you believed before seeing the data, the data updates it, and you get back a range with a probability attached rather than one number. A Gaussian process goes further and puts the distribution directly over functions. The payoff is that the model knows where it is ignorant: the interval widens wherever the data thins out.

Formula
p(β | X, y) ∝ p(y | X, β) · p(β)
Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The output is a distribution, not a point.
f ~ GP(m, K),   posterior mean and variance are closed-form
A GP puts the prior over functions directly rather than over coefficients.
Input → process → output
InputA small or expensive dataset, plus prior beliefs worth encoding.
→
ProcessUpdate the prior with the observed data to get a posterior.
→
OutputA predictive mean and a credible interval everywhere, including where you have no data.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor
from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF

gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(1.0 * RBF(2.0), alpha=3.0, normalize_y=True).fit(Xr, yr)
mu, sd = gp.predict(gridx, return_std=True)

for x in (1.0, 5.0, 9.5, 13.0):
    m_, s_ = gp.predict([[x]], return_std=True)
    inside = "inside the data" if x <= 10 else "EXTRAPOLATING"
    print(f"x = {x:>4}:  {m_[0]:6.2f} ± {2*s_[0]:4.2f}   ({inside})")

print("\nThe interval widens where the data runs out. That is the deliverable.")
show_fit([("GP mean", mu)], "Gaussian process with 95% band", bands=(mu - 2*sd, mu + 2*sd))
Output
x =  1.0:    4.84 ± 1.16   (inside the data)
x =  5.0:    6.59 ± 1.00   (inside the data)
x =  9.5:    5.64 ± 1.18   (inside the data)
x = 13.0:    5.64 ± 1.89   (EXTRAPOLATING)

The interval widens where the data runs out. That is the deliverable.
Look at the last row: asked to predict at x = 13, well past any data, it still answers — but with an interval wide enough to tell you not to trust the number.
In the real world

Bayesian optimisation — tuning an expensive process, a wind-tunnel experiment, a chemical synthesis, or another model's hyperparameters. The uncertainty estimate is what decides where to spend the next costly run: you sample where the model is both promising and unsure. Also standard in geostatistics, where GP regression is called kriging.

Strengths
  • Uncertainty that widens honestly away from the data.
  • Priors let genuine domain knowledge enter the model.
  • Works with very few observations.
  • Enables active learning and Bayesian optimisation.
Limitations
  • GPs cost O(n³) to fit — impractical beyond a few thousand points.
  • Kernel and prior choice materially change the answer.
  • Hierarchical models often need MCMC, which is slow and needs diagnostics.
  • Harder to explain to stakeholders than a coefficient table.

Neighbours & kernels

k-NN regression · kernel ridge · SVR

These methods make no attempt to find an equation. They predict by averaging the training points near you. k-NN takes a plain average of the nearest few; kernel ridge weights every point by distance; SVR fits a tube and ignores anything inside it. All three are local — change the data in one region and the prediction elsewhere barely moves — which is useful when you have no theory about the relationship's shape.

Formula
ŷ(x) = Σ_i w_i(x) · y_i,   Σ w_i = 1
Every method here is a weighted average of training targets. They differ in the weights.
SVR: ignore errors smaller than ε, penalise the rest
The ε-insensitive tube is what makes SVR robust to small noise.
Input → process → output
InputA numeric target with local structure and no known functional form.
→
ProcessWeight nearby training points more heavily — by rank, by kernel, or by support vectors.
→
OutputA smooth interpolation through the data.
Python
Python
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.kernel_ridge import KernelRidge
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

fits = []
for name, est in [("k-NN, k=10", KNeighborsRegressor(10)),
                  ("SVR (RBF)", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVR(C=60, gamma=.2))),
                  ("kernel ridge", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                                                 KernelRidge(alpha=.3, kernel="rbf", gamma=.15)))]:
    m = est.fit(Xr, yr)
    print(f"{name:<13} R² on training data {m.score(Xr, yr):.3f}")
    fits.append((name, m.predict(gridx)))

print("\nNone of these has an equation for the curve. They average what is nearby.")
show_fit(fits, "Three ways of averaging locally")
Output
k-NN, k=10    R² on training data 0.362
SVR (RBF)     R² on training data 0.349
kernel ridge  R² on training data 0.379

None of these has an equation for the curve. They average what is nearby.
In the real world

Process control and soft sensors — inferring a quantity that is expensive to measure directly from several cheap ones, where the physical relationship is smooth but has no tidy closed form. Also widely used for calibration curves in instrumentation, where a local fit beats forcing a global polynomial through the whole range.

Strengths
  • No assumption about the shape of the relationship.
  • k-NN needs no training at all; add data and it is used immediately.
  • SVR's ε-tube ignores small noise rather than chasing it.
  • Kernel ridge has a closed-form solution.
Limitations
  • Prediction cost grows with the training set.
  • All are distance-based, so features must be scaled.
  • Degrade in high dimensions as distances lose meaning.
  • Flat, unreliable extrapolation outside the observed range.

Trees & ensembles

CART · random forest · Extra Trees · gradient boosting · XGBoost · LightGBM · CatBoost

Regression trees chop the feature space into boxes and predict the average of whatever lands in each box. The prediction surface is therefore a staircase, not a curve. That is fine for capturing interactions and sharp thresholds in tabular data, and fatal if you need to predict outside the range you trained on — beyond the data the staircase simply stops, returning the last value it ever learned.

Formula
split to minimise  Σ_left (y − ȳ_L)² + Σ_right (y − ȳ_R)²
The regression analogue of Gini: reduce within-node variance.
ŷ(x) = ȳ of the leaf x falls into
Which is why the prediction surface is a staircase, and flat beyond the data.
Input → process → output
InputTabular features of any type; no scaling, no encoding.
→
ProcessPartition the feature space recursively; average the target in each region.
→
OutputA piecewise-constant prediction, plus feature importances.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor

fits = []
for name, est in [("tree, depth 3", DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=0)),
                  ("random forest", RandomForestRegressor(300, random_state=0)),
                  ("gradient boosting", GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0))]:
    m = est.fit(Xr, yr)
    print(f"{name:<18} R² {m.score(Xr, yr):.3f}")
    fits.append((name, m.predict(gridx)))

far = RandomForestRegressor(300, random_state=0).fit(Xr, yr)
print(f"\ntrained on x up to {Xr.max():.1f}")
for x in (10.0, 20.0, 100.0):
    print(f"  prediction at x = {x:>5}: {far.predict([[x]])[0]:.2f}")
print("Identical. Tree models cannot extrapolate — they return the nearest leaf forever.")
show_fit(fits, "Piecewise-constant fits")
Output
tree, depth 3      R² 0.434
random forest      R² 0.878
gradient boosting  R² 0.960

trained on x up to 10.0
  prediction at x =  10.0: 4.27
  prediction at x =  20.0: 4.27
  prediction at x = 100.0: 4.27
Identical. Tree models cannot extrapolate — they return the nearest leaf forever.
The three predictions at x = 10, 20 and 100 are identical. That is not a bug: a tree can only return the average of a leaf it already built.
In the real world

Demand and price prediction on tabular business data, risk scoring, and sensor-summary regression in predictive maintenance — the same places their classifier counterparts dominate. The extrapolation limit is the thing to watch in practice: a model trained through one winter will not predict a colder one, it will simply return the coldest value it ever saw.

Strengths
  • Captures nonlinearity and interactions with no feature engineering.
  • No scaling or encoding; handles mixed types and missing values.
  • Robust to outliers in the features.
  • Boosted versions are usually the most accurate option on tabular data.
Limitations
  • Cannot extrapolate — predictions flatten outside the training range.
  • The prediction surface is a staircase, which is wrong for smooth physical processes.
  • Large ensembles are memory-hungry and slower to serve.
  • Boosting needs careful validation or it overfits.

Specialised

isotonic regression · PLS · PCR

Isotonic regression fits the best possible curve subject to one hard rule: it can never go down. Where ordinary regression assumes a shape and fits parameters, this assumes only a direction and fits whatever step function satisfies it. You use it when you already know more of an input cannot produce less of an output, and want the model to be incapable of contradicting that.

Formula
minimise Σ (y_i − ŷ_i)² subject to ŷ₁ ≤ ŷ₂ ≤ … ≤ ŷ_n
Least squares with monotonicity as a hard constraint.
PLS: find components of X that covary most with y
Unlike PCA, the target participates in choosing the directions.
Input → process → output
InputA relationship known in advance to be monotonic, or predictors that are many and correlated.
→
ProcessImpose the known structure as a constraint rather than hoping the data reveals it.
→
OutputA fit that cannot violate what you already know.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.isotonic import IsotonicRegression

iso = IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds="clip").fit(Xr[:, 0], yr)
pred = iso.predict(gridx[:, 0])
diffs = np.diff(pred)
print(f"R² {iso.score(Xr[:, 0], yr):.3f}")
print(f"steps that go down: {(diffs < -1e-9).sum()} of {len(diffs)}  (guaranteed zero)")
print(f"\nfitted range: {pred.min():.2f} to {pred.max():.2f}")
print("It never decreases, because it structurally cannot.")
show_fit([("isotonic", pred)], "Isotonic regression")
Output
R² 0.323
steps that go down: 0 of 199  (guaranteed zero)

fitted range: 2.39 to 6.39
It never decreases, because it structurally cannot.
In the real world

Probability calibration — turning an uncalibrated classifier score into something you can read as a probability, where the mapping must be monotonic because a higher score must never mean a lower probability. Also used for dose–response curves and any pricing or scoring model where a regulator requires that more of an input can never reduce the output.

Strengths
  • Enforces monotonicity exactly, not approximately.
  • Non-parametric — no functional form to choose.
  • The standard tool for calibrating classifier outputs.
  • PLS and PCR handle predictors that outnumber observations.
Limitations
  • Isotonic output is a step function, not smooth.
  • Prone to overfitting with little data, since it is very flexible.
  • Only applies where monotonicity genuinely holds.
  • PLS components are harder to interpret than original features.

Forecasting

AR · MA · ARMA · ARIMA · SARIMA/SARIMAX · exponential smoothing · Holt–Winters · VAR · state-space

Forecasting is regression where the ordering of observations is itself information. Yesterday's value tells you about today's, and last December tells you about this one. These methods model that dependence explicitly: autoregressive terms for the influence of recent values, differencing for trend, seasonal terms for cycles. Random train/test splits are invalid here — you must hold out the end of the series, because predicting the past from the future is not forecasting.

Formula
ARIMA(p,d,q): (1 − Σφ_iB^i)(1−B)^d y_t = (1 + Σθ_jB^j) ε_t
B is the backshift operator; d differences away the trend.
SARIMA adds a seasonal term at lag s
s = 24 for hourly data with a daily cycle, 12 for monthly with a yearly one.
Input → process → output
InputA series in time order, long enough to show whatever cycle it has.
→
ProcessDifference to stationarity, fit autoregressive and moving-average terms, model the season.
→
OutputForecasts with prediction intervals that widen as the horizon grows.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, figs

g = np.random.default_rng(1)
t = np.arange(140)
y = 20 + .06*t + 3.4*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/24) + g.normal(0, .9, 140)
train, test = y[:116], y[116:]

naive = train[-24:]                       # seasonal naive: "same hour last cycle"
m = SARIMAX(train, order=(1,1,1), seasonal_order=(1,0,1,24)).fit(disp=False)
f = m.get_forecast(24); mu, ci = f.predicted_mean, f.conf_int()

print(f"seasonal-naive MAE {np.mean(np.abs(test - naive)):.3f}")
print(f"SARIMA        MAE {np.mean(np.abs(test - mu)):.3f}")
print(f"\n95% interval width at h=1: {ci[0,1]-ci[0,0]:.2f}   at h=24: {ci[-1,1]-ci[-1,0]:.2f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 2.6))
ax.plot(t[:116], train, lw=1.2, color=INK2, label="history")
ax.plot(t[116:], test, lw=1.7, color=PALETTE[2], label="actual")
ax.plot(t[116:], mu, lw=1.9, color=PALETTE[4], label="forecast")
ax.fill_between(t[116:], ci[:,0], ci[:,1], color=PALETTE[4], alpha=.18)
ax.legend(ncol=3); ax.set_title("SARIMA, 24 steps ahead", loc="left"); figs.bare(ax)
Output
seasonal-naive MAE 1.389
SARIMA        MAE 1.189

95% interval width at h=1: 4.14   at h=24: 12.34
The MAE comparison is the honest test. Beating seasonal-naive is the bar, and a surprising number of forecasting projects never clear it.
In the real world

Energy load forecasting, retail demand planning, call-centre staffing, cash-flow projection — anywhere the next value depends on recent values and on where you are in a daily, weekly or annual cycle. The discipline that matters most is holding out the *end* of the series, never a random sample, and always reporting against the seasonal-naive baseline.

Strengths
  • Models trend, seasonality and autocorrelation explicitly.
  • Prediction intervals that widen with the horizon, as they should.
  • Interpretable components you can decompose and inspect.
  • Works on short series where machine learning has nothing to learn from.
Limitations
  • Requires stationarity after differencing; p, d, q and s must be chosen.
  • Struggles with abrupt regime changes and one-off events.
  • Classical ARIMA handles one series at a time.
  • External drivers need SARIMAX or a regression-with-lags approach.
04

Unsupervised clustering

Choose a clustering method according to the structure you expect, the feature types you have, and what "similar" should mean. Every panel below runs on the same 316 points: two compact blobs, one elongated band, and scattered noise. That mix is deliberate — it is what separates these methods.

K-means

K-means · MiniBatch K-means

K-means splits data into k groups by repeatedly asking each point which centre it is closest to, then moving each centre to the middle of its members. Two steps, alternated until nothing changes. It is fast and everywhere, and it carries two assumptions you rarely get to escape: you must know k in advance, and every point must belong to some cluster — including the noise.

Formula
minimise  Σ_k Σ_{x ∈ C_k} ‖x − μ_k‖²
Total within-cluster squared distance. The objective is the whole algorithm.
assign: C_k = {x : nearest centre is μ_k}  ·   update: μ_k = mean(C_k)
Alternate the two steps until nothing moves. Converges to a local optimum, not the best one.
Input → process → output
InputNumerical features, scaled, and a chosen k.
→
ProcessAlternate assigning points to the nearest centre and recomputing centres.
→
OutputA hard label for every point and k centroid coordinates.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

for k in range(2, 7):
    km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Xu)
    print(f"k={k}   inertia {km.inertia_:8.1f}   silhouette {silhouette_score(Xu, km.labels_):.3f}")

print("\nInertia always falls as k rises — it can never choose k for you.")
km = KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Xu)
print(f"cluster sizes: {np.bincount(km.labels_)}   (every noise point was absorbed)")
show_clusters(km.labels_, "K-means, k = 4", centers=km.cluster_centers_)
Output
k=2   inertia   2106.4   silhouette 0.515
k=3   inertia    674.1   silhouette 0.682
k=4   inertia    487.1   silhouette 0.628
k=5   inertia    400.1   silhouette 0.631
k=6   inertia    354.3   silhouette 0.537

Inertia always falls as k rises — it can never choose k for you.
cluster sizes: [66 99 96 55]   (every noise point was absorbed)
Silhouette peaks somewhere sensible while inertia simply keeps falling. Picking k by inertia alone always gives you the largest k you tried.
In the real world

Customer segmentation for campaign targeting, where the goal is a handful of groups a marketing team can actually write copy for. Also image colour quantisation, document grouping, and the first pass at operating-regime discovery in industrial telemetry — though in that last case scaling the features correctly matters more than the algorithm choice.

Strengths
  • Fast and scales to millions of rows; MiniBatch handles streaming.
  • Simple to explain, and centroids are directly interpretable.
  • Converges reliably and is available in every toolkit.
  • Works well when clusters genuinely are compact and similarly sized.
Limitations
  • k must be chosen in advance, and nothing in the method tells you what it is.
  • Assumes round, similarly sized clusters; elongated ones get cut in half.
  • Every point is assigned, so noise and outliers distort centroids.
  • Sensitive to initialisation and to feature scaling.

K-medoids

PAM · CLARA · CLARANS

K-medoids is k-means with one change: the centre of each cluster must be a real observation, not an average. That matters when an average is meaningless or unhelpful — you can point at the medoid machine and go inspect it, where you cannot inspect a coordinate that corresponds to nothing. It also frees you from Euclidean distance, since any similarity measure will do.

Formula
minimise  Σ_k Σ_{x ∈ C_k} d(x, m_k),   m_k ∈ dataset
Same shape as k-means, with two differences: any distance d, and the centre must be a real point.
swap m_k with a non-medoid if total cost falls
PAM's partitioning-around-medoids step. Expensive, and the reason CLARA samples.
Input → process → output
InputObservations and any distance function you can define.
→
ProcessChoose k actual observations as centres; swap them while total distance keeps falling.
→
OutputLabels plus k real exemplars you can go and inspect.
Python
Python
import numpy as np

g = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = list(g.choice(len(Xu), 4, replace=False))
for step in range(60):
    d = np.linalg.norm(Xu[:, None] - Xu[idx][None], axis=2)
    lab = d.argmin(1)
    new = []
    for k in range(4):
        members = np.where(lab == k)[0]
        if len(members) == 0:
            new.append(idx[k]); continue
        inner = np.linalg.norm(Xu[members][:, None] - Xu[members][None], axis=2).sum(1)
        new.append(int(members[inner.argmin()]))
    if new == idx:
        print(f"converged after {step} swap rounds"); break
    idx = new

d = np.linalg.norm(Xu[:, None] - Xu[idx][None], axis=2)
print("medoid indices:", idx)
print("medoid coordinates (real observations):\n", Xu[idx].round(2))
show_clusters(d.argmin(1), "K-medoids (PAM)", centers=Xu[idx])
Output
converged after 2 swap rounds
medoid indices: [125, 131, 243, 274]
medoid coordinates (real observations):
 [[-0.19  4.12]
 [-3.97  0.03]
 [ 1.44 -1.14]
 [ 3.2   0.44]]
The medoid coordinates are rows of the dataset, not averages. That is the entire difference from k-means, and in some settings it is the only thing that matters.
In the real world

Patient or case stratification in clinical research, where 'the representative patient for this group' has to be an actual patient whose record can be read, not an average of coordinates that corresponds to nobody. Also used wherever the distance is non-Euclidean — edit distance between sequences, Jaccard between sets, or a hand-built business similarity.

Strengths
  • Centres are real observations you can inspect and show to people.
  • Works with any distance function, including non-metric ones.
  • More robust to outliers than k-means, since medians beat means.
  • Does not require coordinates at all — a distance matrix suffices.
Limitations
  • Much slower than k-means; PAM is roughly quadratic per iteration.
  • Still needs k chosen in advance.
  • CLARA's sampling trades accuracy for the speed it recovers.
  • Not available in scikit-learn — this is a hand-written implementation.

Hierarchical clustering

agglomerative · divisive · Ward/single/complete/average linkage

Hierarchical clustering does not produce one grouping; it produces all of them. Starting from every point alone, it repeatedly merges the two closest clusters and records the height at which each merge happened. The result is a tree you cut wherever you like — cut low for many small groups, high for a few large ones. You decide the number of clusters after seeing the structure rather than before.

Formula
Ward: merge the pair that increases total within-cluster variance least
Other linkages use nearest pair (single), farthest pair (complete) or mean distance (average).
start with n clusters of one point, merge until one remains
The output is the whole merge history, not a single partition.
Input → process → output
InputObservations and a distance plus a linkage rule.
→
ProcessRepeatedly merge the closest pair of clusters, recording the height of each merge.
→
OutputA dendrogram — cut it at any height to get that many groups.
Python
Python
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, figs
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster

Z = linkage(Xu, "ward")
print("the last 5 merges, by height:")
for h in Z[-5:, 2]:
    print(f"  merged at distance {h:.2f}")

for t in (6, 9, 14):
    lab = fcluster(Z, t, criterion="distance")
    print(f"cut at {t:>2}  ->  {len(np.unique(lab))} clusters")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 2.4))
g = np.random.default_rng(0)
dendrogram(linkage(Xu[g.choice(len(Xu), 45, replace=False)], "ward"),
           ax=ax, color_threshold=7, above_threshold_color="#9AA0B8", no_labels=True)
ax.axhline(7, ls="--", lw=1.2, color=PALETTE[4])
ax.set_title("Cut the tree wherever you like", loc="left"); figs.bare(ax)
Output
the last 5 merges, by height:
  merged at distance 9.60
  merged at distance 12.83
  merged at distance 19.24
  merged at distance 54.79
  merged at distance 62.83
cut at  6  ->  12 clusters
cut at  9  ->  8 clusters
cut at 14  ->  4 clusters
Three cut heights give three different clusterings of identical data. The method hands you the whole family and leaves the choice explicitly to you, which is more honest than k-means pretending k was given.
In the real world

Taxonomy building wherever the nesting itself is the finding: gene expression studies, species classification, organisational and product hierarchies, and document topic trees. The dendrogram is also a genuinely good exploratory tool — it shows you the plausible numbers of groups rather than making you guess one up front.

Strengths
  • No need to choose the number of clusters before fitting.
  • The dendrogram shows structure at every scale at once.
  • Deterministic — no random initialisation to worry about.
  • Works from a distance matrix, so any similarity will do.
Limitations
  • O(n²) memory and O(n³) time for the naive algorithm — small data only.
  • Merges are irreversible: an early mistake propagates all the way up.
  • Linkage choice changes the result substantially.
  • Single linkage chains clusters together through thin bridges of points.

Density clustering

DBSCAN · HDBSCAN · OPTICS

Density clustering defines a cluster as a region where points are packed closely together, and anything in the sparse space between as noise. It grows groups outward from points that have enough neighbours nearby, so clusters take whatever shape the data has rather than being forced into round blobs. Crucially, it is allowed to refuse: a point in empty space is labelled noise rather than assigned to the least-bad cluster.

Formula
core point: at least minPts neighbours within ε
Clusters grow by connecting core points; everything unreachable is noise.
HDBSCAN: build the hierarchy over all ε, keep the most stable clusters
Which removes the single most awkward parameter.
Input → process → output
InputObservations, scaled, plus a notion of neighbourhood size.
→
ProcessGrow clusters through dense regions; refuse to assign points in sparse ones.
→
OutputLabels, with −1 meaning 'not in any cluster'.
Python
Python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, HDBSCAN

for eps in (0.4, 0.62, 1.2):
    lab = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=6).fit(Xu).labels_
    n, noise = len(set(lab)) - (1 if -1 in lab else 0), (lab == -1).sum()
    print(f"DBSCAN eps={eps:<5} {n} clusters, {noise:>3} points called noise")

h = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=14).fit(Xu)
nh = len(set(h.labels_)) - (1 if -1 in h.labels_ else 0)
print(f"\nHDBSCAN (no eps)   {nh} clusters, {(h.labels_ == -1).sum()} noise")
print("eps changes DBSCAN's answer completely. HDBSCAN removes the choice.")
show_clusters(DBSCAN(eps=.62, min_samples=6).fit(Xu).labels_, "DBSCAN")
Output
DBSCAN eps=0.4   4 clusters,  66 points called noise
DBSCAN eps=0.62  3 clusters,  26 points called noise
DBSCAN eps=1.2   3 clusters,  12 points called noise

HDBSCAN (no eps)   3 clusters, 14 noise
eps changes DBSCAN's answer completely. HDBSCAN removes the choice.
Three values of ε give three completely different answers on identical data. That sensitivity is DBSCAN's real cost, and the single best argument for HDBSCAN.
In the real world

Geospatial analysis — finding genuine activity hotspots in GPS traces, delivery clusters, or crime incident maps, where most points are scattered background and only dense concentrations matter. Also anomaly detection by proxy: anything DBSCAN refuses to cluster is, by construction, unusual.

Strengths
  • Finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, not just round ones.
  • Explicitly labels noise rather than forcing every point into a group.
  • The number of clusters is an output, not an input.
  • HDBSCAN removes the ε parameter and copes with varying density.
Limitations
